title: Definition and scope
use_cases: Use when distinguishing between science fiction and fantasy based on the source of reality departure
Configure when categorizing literary works for commercial distribution or marketing purposes
Implement when defining the structural requirements for a central love story or mystery puzzle
Use when identifying the historical foundations of specific narrative conventions
content:
Walk into any chain bookstore and the shelves are already making an argument: fantasy lives here, romance lives there, mystery occupies its own corner near the back. That physical sorting reflects something real about how genre fiction works. A genre is a stable cluster of reader expectations — plot shapes, character types, emotional payoffs, and setting conventions — that developed over decades through commercial feedback between publishers, booksellers, and audiences.

The Romance Writers of America defines romance as a story with a central love story and an emotionally satisfying ending (Romance Writers of America). That two-part definition is remarkably precise for something that generates roughly $1.4 billion in annual US book sales (NPD BookScan, cited in Publishers Weekly reporting on genre market share). Mystery fiction, by contrast, is organized around a crime or puzzle and the process of its resolution — a structure codified most visibly in the work of the Detection Club, founded in London in 1930 by writers including Dorothy L. Sayers and G.K. Chesterton.

Science fiction and fantasy occupy the broader speculative fiction space. The key distinction between them: science fiction grounds its departures from reality in extrapolated technology or physical science (however loosely interpreted), while fantasy grounds them in magic, mythology, or supernatural systems. Horror sits adjacent to both, prioritizing emotional dread over resolution.

The commercial genre landscape also includes thrillers, historical fiction, westerns, cozy mysteries, paranormal romance, and cross-genre hybrids. The fiction writing space at large includes both genre and literary fiction, and one of the persistent debates in creative writing circles is whether that distinction tracks anything more meaningful than marketing category.
